Daniel Webster. A dominant figure of nineteenth-century American politics who served as Secretary of State under President William Henry Harrison and John Tyler, and again under Millard Fillmore. He was a gifted orator and skilled diplomat who defended the Union's integrity during the sectional crises leading up to the Civil War while advancing American interests in North America and the Pacific.

Webster first won fame as a Supreme Court advocate. In McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819, he defended federal power against state claims. That same year, in Dartmouth College v. Woodward, he defended the Constitution itself.

He was a pillar of the Whig Party, which favoured a strong federal government and internal improvements over states' rights. When South Carolina threatened to nullify federal tariffs during the Nullification Crisis of the early 1830s, Webster stood firmly against them. His famous Senate speech declared: "Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable."

His greatest diplomatic achievement was negotiating the Webster-Ashburton Treaty in 1842, which resolved the Maine and New Brunswick boundary dispute with Britain and prevented war on the Canadian frontier.

Later, Webster served in the Compromise of 1850, though his support for the Fugitive Slave Act damaged his standing with northern antislavery voters. He championed American expansion in the Pacific and negotiated commercial treaties with Asian powers.

Henry Clay was his great Whig rival and ally, and together they shaped antebellum politics. His intellectual opponent in debates over nullification and federal authority was John C. Calhoun. Webster served as Secretary of State under William Henry Harrison, and the Compromise of 1850 became the capstone to his long career.
